analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.65 an hour by 2004 and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Senator Kennedy with 39 cosponsors, was placed on the Senate calendar in May 2002 but never received a floor vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in three steps: to $5.75 an hour two months after passage, $6.25 on January 1, 2003, and $6.65 on January 1, 2004. It would also, for the first time, apply the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, whose garment factories had been exempt, phasing local wages up from $3.55 to the federal level in 50-cent steps every six months. The bill never came up for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress expired in January 2003.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would see their hourly pay rise from $5.15 to as much as $6.65 by 2004, and workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, whose minimum wage would climb from $3.55 toward the federal level.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.75 within 60 days of enactment, to $6.25 on January 1, 2003, and to $6.65 on January 1, 2004.

Applies federal minimum wage law to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, with a transition starting at $3.55 an hour and rising 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal minimum.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wage, especially small businesses in labor-intensive sectors like restaurants, retail, and the Northern Mariana Islands' garment industry, which would face higher payroll costs; some of the cost may reach consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers and the CNMI garment industry

drawbacks.text: The increases raise payroll costs for employers who pay at or near the minimum wage, with small businesses in low-margin industries facing the largest share of the adjustment.

Extending the federal wage floor to the Northern Mariana Islands — even with the phased transition — increases labor costs sharply for an island economy whose garment factories had operated under a wage far below the federal level, and critics of such rules argued this could accelerate the industry's decline there.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go directly to workers at the bottom of the wage scale, in the form of a roughly 29% raise over three years, while the costs fall on their employers and are partly passed to consumers. The main design caveat is the Northern Mariana Islands provision, which ends a decades-long exemption and would impose an abrupt cost shift on a small island economy despite its gradual phase-in. The wage increase itself is a straightforward transfer from employers to low-paid workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar in May 2002, but no senator ever brought it to the floor for a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on May 22, 2002 with 38 Democratic senators and one Independent as cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill a second time on May 23, 2002 and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 385.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a floor vote, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the $5.15 minimum wage — including restaurants, retail chains, and the Northern Mariana Islands' garment factories — kept the existing wage floor because the bill never came to a vote despite the support of 40 senators.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who pay the minimum wage

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2002 in the Senate on May 22, 2002.

for.name: 38 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the backing of more than three-quarters of the Senate's Democratic caucus.

against.name: Jack Abramoff
against.role: Lobbyist for the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for years on behalf of the Northern Mariana Islands government to keep its garment industry exempt from the federal minimum wage — the very exemption this bill would have ended.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken, so there is no vote record; support on the calendar was almost entirely Democratic — 38 of 49 Senate Democrats plus one Independent cosponsored, and no Republican did — but the Democratic majority never scheduled the bill for a floor vote either.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, and other minimum-wage businesses)
industries.note: The three-step increase to $6.65 raises payroll costs for businesses that pay at or near the minimum wage. For workers whose pay would have risen about 29% by 2004, the industry's interest in keeping the bill off the floor runs directly against theirs.

The bill ends the territory's decades-long exemption from federal wage law, phasing factory wages up from $3.55 toward the federal minimum. The industry's sub-federal wage advantage — preserved through an extended lobbying campaign — existed because garment workers were paid far less than the federal floor.
